unit-tkam-c08.title: To Kill a Mockingbird · Ch. 8: Snow, Fire and a Blanket
unit-tkam-c08.source: To Kill a Mockingbird (Harper Lee), chapter quiz — chapter 8

summary.text: Chapter 8 of To Kill a Mockingbird: a rare snow closes school, and Mr. Avery blames it on badly behaved children. Jem builds a mud-and-snow snowman that looks like Mr. Avery until Atticus has him disguise it. That night Miss Maudie's house burns down. While the neighbors fight the fire, someone puts a blanket around Scout without her noticing; Atticus works out it was Boo Radley, and Jem tells him everything about the pants and the knothole. The next day Miss Maudie is cheerful about her loss.

why.text: Boo steps out among the whole town and does something kind, and nobody sees him. That is the strongest evidence so far that the legend is wrong.

objectives.text: Retell the snow day, the snowman and the fire in order.
Explain why Atticus calls the snowman a near libel.
Explain what the blanket reveals about Boo, and why Jem tells Atticus everything.
Describe how Miss Maudie responds to losing her house, and what that shows.

parentNote.text: This quiz covers chapter 8 only and stops at the end of that chapter, the day after Miss Maudie's fire. There is a house fire, though nobody is hurt; it is not graphic. The thing most likely to trip her up is the blanket: she needs to see why Atticus concludes it was Boo, and why Jem suddenly tells him everything. The ponder card about being quietly looked after is a good one for dinner.

nextUp.text: Finish chapter 8, then run the cards and the quiz.

cards.def:
**A rare snow falls on Maycomb and school is closed for the day.**
• Scout has never seen snow and first thinks the world is ending.
• Mr. Avery blames the change in the weather on children who misbehave.
cards.hint: To a Southern town, snow is close to a miracle; to Mr. Avery, it is a punishment.

cards.def:
**There isn't enough snow for a real snowman, so Jem builds one from mud and covers it with snow — and it looks just like Mr. Avery.**
• Jem is proud of his engineering.
• The likeness to a real neighbor is the problem.
cards.hint: Mud underneath, snow on top: Jem solves the shortage like a builder.

cards.def:
**A false or damaging portrayal of a real person that hurts his reputation.**
• Atticus calls the snowman a near libel: it mocks Mr. Avery for all to see.
• He has Jem disguise it, and Jem adds Miss Maudie's sun hat and hedge clippers.
cards.hint: Libel is damage done to a name, in words or pictures.

cards.def:
**On the coldest night, Miss Maudie's house catches fire and burns down.**
• The neighbors carry her furniture out into the street.
• Atticus sends Jem and Scout to stand by the Radley gate, out of the way.
cards.hint: The whole street turns out for one neighbor.

cards.def:
**While Scout watches the fire, someone puts a blanket around her shoulders — and she never notices.**
• Back home, Atticus asks where the blanket came from.
• He works out that it must have been Boo Radley.
cards.hint: Scout was standing right in front of the Radley house.

cards.def:
**Afraid Boo will get in trouble, Jem tells Atticus everything: the pants, the knothole gifts, the cement.**
• It all comes out at once.
• Jem is now defending Boo, not hunting him.
cards.hint: Jem stops keeping secrets from Atticus once Boo needs protecting.

cards.def:
**Miss Maudie is cheerful: she always wanted a smaller house, and now she'll have more room for her azaleas.**
• She has lost almost everything and refuses to mourn it.
• Her attitude surprises Scout more than the fire did.
cards.hint: Ask what Miss Maudie cares about more than her house.

cards.def:
**Too deep or strange to understand.**
• The chapter opens by calling the cold snap unfathomable, even to the town's most experienced weather prophets.
• A fathom is a measure of water depth, so unfathomable means too deep to measure.
cards.hint: If you cannot measure how deep it goes, you cannot get to the bottom of it.

cards.def:
**Would you want to know if someone had been quietly looking out for you without your noticing?**
• Think about how Scout feels when she learns about the blanket.
• There is no single right answer to this one.
cards.hint: A dinner-table question: gratitude, or a shiver, or both?

questions.q: How does Jem build a snowman when there isn't enough snow?
opts: He shapes a figure out of mud and covers it with snow
He carves a figure out of ice from the town icehouse
He waits two days for more snow to fall before building
He makes a much smaller one with the snow there is
questions.hint: He uses what Maycomb has plenty of.
steps: There is not enough snow for a whole snowman.
Jem has dirt and mud to work with instead.
He builds the body from mud.
Then he covers the mud figure with snow.

ex.main: **He shapes it from mud and covers it with snow.** It is clever, and it is also why the snowman can be shaped so precisely into a real person.
ex.tip: When a character solves a problem cleverly, look for the trouble the solution causes next.

questions.q: Whose house burns down in chapter 8?
opts: Miss Stephanie Crawford's
Miss Maudie Atkinson's
Miss Rachel Haverford's
Mr. Avery's boarding house
questions.hint: She loves her garden more than her house.
steps: The fire breaks out on the coldest night of the winter.
The neighbors carry furniture out of a house on the Finches' street.
It is the house of the neighbor the children like best.
It is Miss Maudie Atkinson's house.

ex.main: **Miss Maudie Atkinson's.** The fire tests her, and the next morning shows what she is made of.
ex.tip: Recall questions are easier when you tie each event to the character it changes.

questions.q: Who does Atticus conclude put the blanket around Scout's shoulders?
opts: Mr. Avery
Mr. Nathan Radley
Boo Radley
Miss Stephanie
steps: Scout was standing in front of the Radley house.
She never saw who covered her.
Everyone else Atticus could think of was busy with the fire.
Atticus concludes it was Boo Radley.

ex.main: **Boo Radley.** He came out among the whole town during the fire, and nobody saw him.
ex.tip: Use where a character was standing as evidence; setting is often a clue.

questions.q: Atticus calls Jem's snowman "a near libel" and has him disguise it. Why?
opts: It might frighten the younger children on the street
It is built on land that belongs to Miss Maudie
It uses mud, which Atticus thinks is too messy
It mocks a real neighbor in a way anyone could recognise
questions.hint: Who does the snowman look like?
steps: Libel means damaging a real person's reputation.
The snowman is shaped to look like Mr. Avery.
Anyone walking by would recognise who it mocks.
So Atticus has Jem disguise it, to spare a real neighbor.

ex.main: **It mocks a real neighbor in a way anyone could recognise.** Atticus treats even a joke about Mr. Avery as something that can hurt a person's name.
ex.tip: When a character uses a legal word for an everyday situation, ask what serious principle he is pointing to.

questions.q: Put these chapter 8 events in the order they happen.
opts: Snow falls on Maycomb and school is closed
Jem builds a snowman that looks like Mr. Avery
Miss Maudie's house catches fire in the night
Miss Maudie says she always wanted a smaller house
steps: The chapter opens with the cold and the snow.
Jem builds the snowman during the snow day.
The fire comes that night, the coldest of the winter.
Miss Maudie's cheerful answer comes the next day.

ex.main: **Snow → snowman → fire → Miss Maudie's answer.** A strange, playful day turns into a frightening night, and ends on a lesson in resilience.
ex.tip: Use time markers — day, night, next morning — to sort the events of a chapter.

questions.q: After the fire, Jem suddenly tells Atticus all about the pants and the knothole. What makes him do it?
opts: He is afraid Boo will get in trouble for the blanket
He wants Atticus to punish Mr. Nathan for the cement
He thinks Atticus already knows everything anyway
He wants to boast about how brave the raid had been
questions.hint: Who does Jem want to protect now?
steps: Atticus has just worked out that Boo put the blanket on Scout.
Jem fears Boo could be blamed for coming out.
To show Boo means no harm, he explains everything Boo has done.
So he tells all because he is afraid Boo will get in trouble.

ex.main: **He is afraid Boo will get in trouble.** Jem has moved from daring Boo to defending him.
ex.tip: When a character changes sides, mark the moment; it is usually what the chapter is about.

questions.q: The chapter calls the cold weather "unfathomable" to the town's weather prophets. What does unfathomable mean?
opts: Easy to see coming from far away
Too deep or strange to understand
Dangerous to anyone left outside
Expected at that time every year
questions.hint: A fathom measures how deep water is.
steps: A fathom is a unit for measuring water depth.
Un- means not, and -able means can be.
So unfathomable means something whose depth cannot be measured.
In other words: too deep or strange to understand.

ex.main: **Too deep or strange to understand.** Even the people who claim to predict the weather cannot explain this winter.
ex.tip: Break a long word into prefix, root and suffix before guessing.

questions.passage: For reasons unfathomable to the most experienced prophets in Maycomb County, autumn turned to winter that year.

questions.q: Boo walks among the whole town during the fire and puts a blanket on Scout, and nobody sees him. What does that suggest?
opts: Scout was so cold that she fell asleep standing up
Boo has secretly been leaving his house every single night
People see what they expect, and no one expects a kind Boo
The town has decided to stop gossiping about the Radleys
questions.hint: Everyone is looking for a monster.
steps: The whole street is out, and Boo walks right through it.
He does something gentle and practical: he keeps a child warm.
No one notices, because no one imagines Boo doing that.
So people see what they expect, and nobody expects a kind Boo.

ex.main: **People see what they expect.** The town's legend is so strong that Boo can be kind in plain view without anyone noticing.
ex.tip: When a character goes unseen in a crowd, ask what the crowd was looking for instead.

questions.q: Miss Maudie loses her house and says she always wanted a smaller one, with more room for her azaleas. What does this show about her?
opts: She does not yet understand how much she has lost
She is hiding how angry she is at the fire department
She never liked her neighbors and wants to move away
She values her garden and her spirit over her belongings
steps: Her house and most of her things are gone.
She talks about her flowers and the space she has now.
She chooses to look at what is left, not at what burned.
She values her garden and her spirit over her belongings.

ex.main: **She values her garden and her spirit over her belongings.** Her cheerfulness is a choice, and it teaches Scout more than any lecture could.
ex.tip: When a character reacts to disaster in an unexpected way, the reaction is the clue to her character.

questions.q: Mr. Avery blames the snow on children who misbehave. How does the chapter treat that idea?
opts: As a superstition that the story gently pokes fun at
As the real cause, since the snow follows the raid
As Atticus's own belief, which he teaches the children
As a warning that the children take very seriously
questions.hint: Who in this book tends to be right about the world?
steps: Mr. Avery claims children's bad behavior changes the seasons.
The narrator reports it the way she reports other Maycomb superstitions.
Atticus, the book's steady voice, never backs it.
So the chapter treats it as a superstition to smile at.

ex.main: **As a superstition the story gently pokes fun at.** It is another example of Maycomb explaining what it does not understand with a story that sounds certain.
ex.tip: Notice whose explanations the narrator trusts; the others are often there to be questioned.
